z-m-21-01.title: The conclusion "only one": is it really the only one?
z-m-21-01.topic: Writing a degree-4 expression as a product of two quadratic expressions: checking every possible case
z-m-21-01.goal: Check the conclusion "only one" that was drawn after looking at only some of the possible cases, make different products of quadratic expressions for the same degree-4 expression to confirm it, and explain why the number of ways is fixed even when the conditions are widened.
z-m-21-01.material: Jiho found a way to write x⁴−5x²+4 in the form (x²+ax+b)(x²+cx+d). Here the coefficient of x² is 1 in both quadratic expressions, a, b, c, d are integers, and swapping the order of the two quadratic expressions (for example, swapping a, b with c, d) counts as the same factorization. After finishing the solution, Jiho said, "There is only one such factorization." Below is Jiho's solution. (How to read: x⁴ is "x to the fourth power", x² is "x squared", and ac is "a times c".)
z-m-21-01.thinking.0: Finding the line where a case was left out
z-m-21-01.thinking.1: Making different examples of your own that break the conclusion
z-m-21-01.thinking.2: Judging how the conclusion changes when the condition is changed (integers to real numbers)
z-m-21-01.prereq.0: Expanding the product of two quadratic expressions and organizing terms of the same degree (level of the polynomial unit in Common Math, middle school grade 3 to high school grade 1)
z-m-21-01.prereq.1: The meaning of two polynomials being the same expression in x (an identity). The grade placement of this activity is only a difficulty division within the production batch and not a grade assignment in the curriculum
z-m-21-01.prereq.2: Experience of expanding a product of linear expressions such as (x−1), (x+1)
z-m-21-01.s.s1.prompt: Which line makes Jiho's conclusion "only one" hard to believe as it is? Choose one line.
z-m-21-01.s.s1.hint.0: Mark whether each line follows directly from the line just before it, and from which line the phrase "this is the only one" first appears.
z-m-21-01.s.s1.hint.1: List all the integer pairs whose product is 4 yourself, and compare them one by one with the list in line 4.
z-m-21-01.s.s1.line.0: Expand (x²+ax+b)(x²+cx+d) and match the coefficient of each degree so that it becomes the same expression as x⁴−5x²+4.
z-m-21-01.s.s1.line.1: From the coefficient of x³, a+c=0, so c=−a, and from the coefficient of x, ad+bc=a(d−b)=0, so a=0 or b=d.
z-m-21-01.s.s1.line.3: b and d are integers and their product is 4, so (b, d) is one of (1, 4), (4, 1), (2, 2).
z-m-21-01.s.s1.line.4: Among these, the only one that satisfies the x² coefficient b+d−a²=−5 is b=d=2, a=3 (or a=−3).
z-m-21-01.s.s1.line.5: Therefore, (x²+3x+2)(x²−3x+2) is the only such factorization.
z-m-21-01.s.s1.explain: The calculations in lines 1 to 3 are correct (the coefficient of x² is b+d+ac, and since c=−a, it is b+d−a²). Line 4 is where it first goes wrong. Integer pairs with product 4 also include (−1, −4), (−4, −1), (−2, −2), but only the positive pairs were written. Line 5 is correct "within the list that was written", but the list is incomplete, so "only one" in line 6 lacks support. Even if you chose line 6, the issue is not the calculation of that line itself but "whether all cases were checked earlier".
z-m-21-01.s.s2.prompt: Make two different factorizations (x²+ax+b)(x²+cx+d) that equal x⁴−5x²+4. (a, b, c, d are integers. Ones that differ only in order count as the same factorization.)
z-m-21-01.s.s2.hint.0: Start by testing the side Jiho missed. Among the integer pairs with product 4, choose a negative pair and plug in one by one to see whether the remaining coefficient conditions hold.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.hint.1: Split into two branches, the case a=0 and the case b=d, and find the values of b and d in each.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.var.a: a (the x coefficient of the first expression)
z-m-21-01.s.s2.var.b: b (the constant term of the first expression)
z-m-21-01.s.s2.var.c: c (the x coefficient of the second expression)
z-m-21-01.s.s2.var.d: d (the constant term of the second expression)
z-m-21-01.s.s2.ok.c0: a, b, c, d are all integers.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.fail.c0: Please take a, b, c, d to be integers.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The coefficient of x³ (a+c) after expanding is not 0.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.fail.c2: The coefficient of x² (b+d+ac) after expanding is not −5.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The coefficient of x (ad+bc) after expanding is not 0.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.fail.c4: The constant term (bd) after expanding is not 4.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.explain: There are three possible integer factorizations: (x²−1)(x²−4), (x²+3x+2)(x²−3x+2), and (x²+x−2)(x²−x−2). Jiho's factorization is just one of them. Ones that differ only in order, like swapping a and −a, were counted as the same factorization.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.because.prompt: If two different groupings both make x⁴−5x²+4, where did Jiho's conclusion "only one" go wrong? Write two or three sentences, using at least one of the expressions you just made.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: Expand each of the two groupings you made and compare whether the results are the same expression.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Compare how Jiho organized the possible cases and whether the groupings you made are in that list.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you check yourself that the expression you gave really becomes x⁴−5x²+4 when expanded?
z-m-21-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you point out the cause of the mistake as "leaving out possible cases" rather than a "calculation mistake"?
z-m-21-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you also write what must be done to say "only one"?
z-m-21-01.s.s2.because.model.0: Expanding (x²−1)(x²−4) gives x⁴−5x²+4, and expanding (x²+3x+2)(x²−3x+2) also gives the same expression. Both groupings are correct, so it is not the only one. Jiho left out the negative pairs among the integer pairs with product 4, so only one was left.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.because.modelNote.0: Mentions both the counterexample (another grouping) and the cause (leaving out cases)
z-m-21-01.s.s2.because.model.1: x⁴−5x²+4 can be written as (x−1)(x+1)(x−2)(x+2), so depending on how you group the four linear expressions in pairs, many products of quadratic expressions come out, such as (x²+x−2)(x²−x−2). Jiho's conclusion comes from finding only one way without checking all the cases.
z-m-21-01.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: Explained from another viewpoint, grouping linear expressions
z-m-21-01.s.s3.prompt: Now let's widen the condition "integer coefficients" to "real coefficients" (two quadratic expressions whose x² coefficient is 1; ones that differ only in order are the same factorization). The coefficient conditions above, a+c=0, a(d−b)=0, b+d−a²=−5, bd=4, can be used as they are. What is the most fitting statement about the number of possible factorizations in this case?
z-m-21-01.s.s3.hint.0: Start from a(d−b)=0, split into the case a=0 and the case b=d, and write the equations left in each.
z-m-21-01.s.s3.hint.1: In each branch, solve directly and count how many values b and d can take when they are real numbers.
z-m-21-01.s.s3.o.a: There are far more real numbers than integers, so there are infinitely many factorizations
z-m-21-01.s.s3.r.a: This thinking sees that when the allowed numbers increase, the answers increase too. But in this case, how about first thinking about how the coefficient conditions tie a, b, c, d together?
z-m-21-01.s.s3.o.b: It becomes fewer than with integers. Real numbers include integers, so the conditions are stricter
z-m-21-01.s.s3.r.b: You drew the opposite conclusion from the fact that "real numbers include integers". When the allowed range gets wider, the possible factorizations cannot decrease. Check whether the three from the integer case still work.
z-m-21-01.s.s3.o.c: It is still three. In the two branches (the case a=0 and the case b=d), the values are already fixed
z-m-21-01.s.s3.r.c: This judgment splits into two branches and checks whether the values are fixed in the real numbers as well.
z-m-21-01.s.s3.o.d: The conditions are not enough, so we cannot say how many there are
z-m-21-01.s.s3.r.d: This judgment says "not enough information" without counting whether the four given equations are enough. Check whether four unknowns and four equations narrow down the values.
z-m-21-01.s.s3.explain: Since a(d−b)=0, a=0 or b=d. If a=0, then b+d=−5 and bd=4, so b and d are only the two roots −1 and −4 of t²+5t+4=0. If b=d, then b²=4 gives b=±2, and a²=2b+5, so when b=2, a=±3, and when b=−2, a=±1. Even in the real numbers there is nothing outside these branches, so ignoring order there are still three. The condition of being an integer did not play the role of filtering in this case.
